{{Short description|Measure of spacial autocorrelation}}
{{DISPLAYTITLE:Geary's ''C''}}
'''Geary's ''C''''' is a measure of spatial [[autocorrelation]] developed by [[Roy C. Geary]].<ref>{{Cite journal
 | doi = 10.2307/2986645
 | author = [[Roy C. Geary|Geary, R. C.]]
 | year = 1954
 | title = The Contiguity Ratio and Statistical Mapping
 | journal = [[The Incorporated Statistician]]
 | volume = 5
 | pages = 115&ndash;145
 | jstor = 2986645
 | issue = 3
}}</ref> that attempts to determine if observations of the same variable are spatially autocorrelated globally (rather than at the neighborhood level). [[Spatial autocorrelation]] is more complex than [[autocorrelation]] because the correlation is multi-dimensional and bi-directional.

== Global Geary's C ==

The generalised Geary coefficient<ref name = "cliff-ord">{{cite book | last1= Cliff |first1= A. D. | last2= Ord |first2= J. K. |orig-year= 1981 |chapter= Measures of autocorrelation in the plane |title= Spatial processes: models & applications |publication-place= [[London]] |publisher= Pion Limited |at= 1.4.1 The form of the coefficients (p. 17) |isbn= 0-85086-081-4}}</ref> is defined as

:<math> C = \frac{(N-1) \sum_{i} \sum_{j} w_{ij} (x_i-x_j)^2}{2 S_0 \sum_{i}(x_i-\bar x)^2} </math>

where <math>N</math> is the number of spatial units indexed by <math>i</math> and <math>j</math>; <math>x</math> is the variable of interest; <math>\bar x</math> is the mean of <math>x</math>; <math>w_{ij}</math> is the <math>i^{th}</math> row of the spatial weights matrix <math>W</math> with zeroes on the diagonal (i.e., <math>w_{ii} = 0</math>); and <math>S_0</math> is the sum of all weights in <math>W</math>.

[[File:Geary example.png|thumb|Geary's C statistic computed for different spatial patterns. Using '[[Rook (chess)|rook]]' neighbors for each grid cell, setting <math>w_{ij}=1</math> for neighbours  <math>j</math> of <math>i</math> and then row normalizing the weight matrix. Top left shows gives <math>C>1</math> indicating anti-correlation. Top right shows a spatial gradient giving <math>C<1</math> indicating correlation. Bottom left shows random data giving a value of <math>C\sim1</math> indicating no correlation. Bottom right shows a spreading pattern with positive autocorrelation.
]]

The value of Geary's ''C'' lies between 0 and some unspecified value greater than 1. Values significantly lower than 1 demonstrate increasing positive spatial autocorrelation, whilst values significantly higher than 1 illustrate increasing negative spatial autocorrelation.

Geary's ''C'' is inversely related to [[Moran's I|Moran's ''I'']], but it is not identical. While Moran's ''I'' and Geary's ''C'' are both measures of global spatial autocorrelation, they are slightly different. Geary's ''C'' uses the sum of squared distances whereas Moran's ''I'' uses standardized spatial covariance. By using squared distances Geary's ''C'' is less sensitive to linear associations and may pickup autocorrelation where Moran's ''I'' may not.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Anselin |first1=Luc |title=A Local Indicator of Multivariate Spatial Association: Extending Geary's c |journal=Geographical Analysis |date=April 2019 |volume=51 |issue=2 |pages=133–150 |doi=10.1111/gean.12164|doi-access=free }}</ref>

Geary's ''C'' is also known as Geary's contiguity ratio or simply Geary's ratio.<ref>{{cite journal
| doi = 10.2307/2986827
| author = J. N. R. Jeffers 
| year = 1973
| title = A Basic Subroutine for Geary's Contiguity Ratio
| publisher = Wiley
| journal = Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series D
| volume = 22
| issue = 4
| pages = 299–302 
| jstor = 2986827 
}}</ref>

==Local Geary's C==

Like [[Moran's I]], Geary's C can be decomposed into a sum of Local Indicators of Spatial Association (LISA) statistics. LISA statistics can be used to find local clusters through [[Statistical hypothesis test|significance testing]], though because a large number of tests must be performed (one per sampling area) this approach suffers from the [[multiple comparisons problem]]. As noted by [[Luc Anselin|Anselin]],<ref>{{cite web | url=https://geodacenter.github.io/workbook/6b_local_adv/lab6b.html#local-geary | title=Local Spatial Autocorrelation (2) }}</ref> this means the analysis of the local Geary statistic is aimed at identifying ''interesting'' points which should then be subject to further investigation. This is therefore a type of [[exploratory data analysis]].

A local version of <math>C</math> is given by<ref>{{Cite journal
 | doi = 10.1111/gean.12164
 | author = [[Luc Anselin|Anselin, L.]]
 | year = 2019
 | title = A local indicator of multivariate spatial association: extending Geary's C
 | journal = Geographical Analysis
 | volume = 51
 | issue = 2
 | pages = 133–150
}}
</ref>
:<math>c_i = \frac{1}{m_2}\sum_j w_{ij}(x_i-x_j)^2</math>
where
:<math> m_2= \frac{\sum_i (x_i-\bar x)^2 }{N-1}</math>
then,
:<math> C = \sum_i \frac{c_i}{2S_0} </math>

Local Geary's C can be calculated in [[GeoDa]] and [[PySAL]].<ref>{{cite web | url=https://pysal.org/esda/ | title=ESDA: Exploratory Spatial Data Analysis — esda v2.6.0 Manual }}</ref>
